notes: Prosecutor's case stated on admissibility of consent blood sample taken before drink-driving suspicion; Laws LJ applied s15(2) RTOA 1988 amendment.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Carless: admissibility of pre-suspicion alcohol blood sample
key_facts: After a high-speed M26 crash the driver walked away; blood from inside the overturned car matched DNA taken when he was treated as an abduction victim.
The respondent gave consent blood and urine samples nine hours later during a kidnapping investigation, not under section 7 drink-driving procedure.
Analysis showed 95mg alcohol per 100ml blood, above the limit, but magistrates excluded the sample as inadmissible in law and acquitted.
The prosecutor appealed by case stated on whether section 15(2), as amended by the Road Traffic Act 1991, displaced Howard v Hallett.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecutor's appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' acquittal on a drink-driving charge after exclusion of blood evidence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the blood sample was admissible under section 15(2) even though not taken in connection with the alleged offence; matter remitted to magistrates to continue the trial.
enrichment.ratio: Section 15(2) of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988, as amended, expressly permits evidence of alcohol in specimens not provided or taken in connection with the alleged offence; Howard v Hallett still governs specimens taken in connection with the offence, and section 78 PACE may exclude otherwise admissible samples on fairness grounds.
legal_issues: Whether a consent blood sample taken before drink-driving was suspected is admissible under section 15(2)
Whether Howard v Hallett and Murray v DPP remain applicable after the 1991 amendment
Whether section 15(4) applies where the section 15(2) parenthesis is engaged
Whether magistrates were correct to exclude the evidence as a matter of law
linked_authorities: Howard v Hallett [1984] RTR 353
Murray v DPP (1994) 158 JPR 261

notes: Planning appeal quashed because inspector failed to address whether two mobile homes with timber extensions were caravans for gypsy status.

enrichment.short_title: Green v inspector: gypsy site permission quashed over caravan definition

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Shane Jones and his extended Romany family occupied Moate Farm, Canterbury, in three mobile living units after council deferral of a retrospective gypsy site application.
Canterbury refused permission and issued enforcement notices; an inspector granted deemed permission for three units subject to personal and landscaping conditions.
The claimant challenged gypsy status, countryside policies, personal circumstances and Article 8, but succeeded only on the definition of the structures on site.
Two units comprised caravans bolted to timber extensions; the council's licensing officer had doubted they remained caravans under the statutory definition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court statutory review of an inspector's decision on linked planning and enforcement appeals for a private gypsy caravan site.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and the inspector's decision quashed because she failed to address whether all three units were caravans, a material consideration for gypsy status and the permission granted; leave to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: Where objectors contend that dwellings on a gypsy site fall outside the statutory caravan definition, especially where units are composite structures incapable of movement as a single unit following Carter, the inspector must address that issue with reasons; failure to do so vitiates the decision even if other grounds fail.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector could reasonably find Shane Jones retained gypsy status
Whether mobile homes with timber extensions qualified as caravans
Whether the inspector adequately applied countryside and conservation policies
Whether personal healthcare needs justified overriding countryside harm
linked_authorities: Wrexham County Borough Council v National Assembly for Wales [2003] EWCA Civ 835
Carter v Secretary of State for the Environment [1994] 1 WLR 1212
Basildon v Secretary of State [2001] JPL 1184

notes: Court of Appeal applied Razgar to uphold clearly unfounded certificate for Dublin transfer of Somali asylum seeker to Italy.

enrichment.short_title: G v SSHD: Dublin removal and clearly unfounded Article 8 certificate
key_facts: G, a Somali, claimed asylum in Italy in July 2003 then in the UK in September 2003 with a false recent arrival date.
Italy was designated the responsible state; the Secretary of State certified her human rights claim as clearly unfounded under section 93, denying an in-country appeal.
She later claimed to be a minor born in 1988 and relied on brief family life with a cousin, Mrs S, supported by paediatric and statutory declaration evidence.
Wilson J dismissed judicial review; the Court of Appeal reapplied the Razgar predictive test to the certificate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from dismissal of judicial review of a section 93 clearly unfounded certificate blocking in-country appeal against Dublin removal to Italy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; even applying Razgar and considering later evidence, removal to Italy would be in accordance with the law and proportionate, so the certificate challenge must fail.
enrichment.ratio: Article 15 of Regulation 343/2003 does not confer a freestanding substantive right on an asylum seeker to remain in a second Member State; it regulates inter-state cooperation, and on Razgar analysis a hypothetical adjudicator would find Dublin removal lawful and proportionate despite arguable family life with a cousin.
legal_issues: Whether Article 15 Dublin II prevents removal to the responsible Member State
Application of the Razgar questions to a clearly unfounded certificate
Whether family life with a cousin and minor status make removal disproportionate
Whether Wilson J adopted the wrong standard of review
linked_authorities: R (Razgar) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] UKHL 27
Costello-Roberts v United Kingdom (1993) 19 EHRR 112

notes: Workplace Regulations reg 5 held not to apply to burst concealed pipe causing wet floor slip at nursing home.

enrichment.short_title: Lewis v Avidan: regulation 5 and burst pipe workplace slip
key_facts: Wendy Lewis, a care assistant at High Meadow Nursing Home, slipped on a wet linoleum floor at about 6am after a concealed pipe burst.
No one knew of the leak before the accident; the judge found no negligence or occupiers' liability breach and no breach of regulations 8 or 12.
Regulation 5 imposes an absolute duty to maintain the workplace in efficient state, working order and good repair.
The judge held regulation 5 did not apply because the pipe was not workplace or qualifying equipment and a burst would not itself breach other regulations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave from dismissal of an employer's liability claim after split trial on liability in the County Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; regulation 5 did not apply to the burst pipe, the floor remained maintained in efficient state despite temporary flooding, and regulation 12(3) required reasonable practicability not absolute liability for wet floors.
enrichment.ratio: An enclosed burst water pipe is not part of the workplace definition and, even if equipment under regulation 5(3)(a), a fault liable to wet a floor does not itself result in failure to comply with regulation 12(3) or 5(1); an unexpected flood does not mean the floor is not maintained in efficient state following Latimer.
legal_issues: Whether a concealed burst pipe is workplace or equipment under regulation 5
Whether regulations 5 and 12(3) are mutually exclusive
Whether a burst pipe fault is liable to result in breach of other regulations
Whether temporary wetting from unforeseeable flooding breaches regulation 5(1)
linked_authorities: Latimer v AEC Ltd [1953] AC 643
Stark v The Post Office [2000] PIQR 105
Beck v United Closures and Plastics Ltd (2001) SLT 1299

notes: Interim housing JR adjourned; Sheffield ordered to fund Westminster accommodation pending County Court appeal on section 193 duty.

enrichment.short_title: R W v Sheffield: interim housing for vulnerable homeless man

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: RW, a 51-year-old man with learning disability, low IQ and serious mental health problems, was referred by Westminster to Sheffield as having a local connection there.
He had briefly lived in Sheffield 2001-2004 but now engaged with The Passage day centre in Westminster and refused to return to Sheffield, exhibiting suicidal ideation.
Sheffield accepted the section 193 referral but offered accommodation only in Sheffield; Beatson J ordered interim Westminster accommodation at Sheffield's expense.
A Westminster section 204 appeal was listed for 28 April 2005; Gibbs J adjourned the judicial review and continued interim funding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim judgment in judicial review of Sheffield's refusal to secure suitable accommodation in Westminster for a priority-need homeless person.
enrichment.outcome: Claim adjourned; Sheffield to continue providing temporary accommodation in Westminster until disposal of the County Court appeal or further order, with expedited transcript for that hearing; no final findings made.
enrichment.ratio: Where a vulnerable homeless person has credible support only in Westminster and cannot realistically return to the referring authority's area, an exceptional case may warrant judicial review despite County Court appeal routes; interim relief preserving accommodation pending the section 204 appeal can be justified without concluded rulings on suitability of location.
legal_issues: Whether Sheffield's section 193 duty extends to securing accommodation outside its area
Whether Westminster's local connection finding was irrational
Whether judicial review is appropriate where section 204 appeal is pending
Whether accommodation in Sheffield can be suitable given the claimant's vulnerability

notes: Court of Appeal upheld exercise of section 33 discretion to allow out-of-time VWF claim against council employer.

enrichment.short_title: Burgin v Sheffield: section 33 discretion in VWF limitation appeal
key_facts: The respondent claimed vibration white finger from use of vibratory tools while employed by Sheffield City Council (1964-1992) and a later employer (1994-2001).
The claim against the Council was issued in March 2003; the judge found relevant knowledge by 1992 or at latest 1995 but exercised section 33 discretion to disapply limitation.
The Council conceded causation would be no harder to prove than if the claim were in time but argued prejudice on apportionment and loss of supervisor evidence.
Supervisor Tom Slater had died but other Council witnesses remained available.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a County Court preliminary issue decision allowing an out-of-time personal injury claim to proceed under section 33.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge did not err in principle or exceed the generous ambit of reasonable disagreement in finding no significant evidential prejudice and that equity required the claim to proceed against both employers.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 33(3)(b) the evidential burden of showing cogency prejudice from delay lies on the defendant; where a defendant fails to adduce convincing prejudice evidence, especially on apportionment between successive employers using similar vibratory tools, an appellate court will not interfere with a judge's equitable discretion to allow the claim.
legal_issues: Whether the claimant had date of knowledge by 1992 or 1995
Allocation of evidential burden under section 33(3)(b)
Whether loss of a deceased supervisor's evidence caused significant prejudice
Whether apportionment difficulties justify refusing section 33 relief
linked_authorities: Hartley v Birmingham City District Council [1992] 1 WLR 968
KR v Bryn Alyn Community (Holdings) Ltd [2003] QB 144
G v G (Minors: Custody Appeal) [1985] 1 WLR 647

notes: Clearly unfounded certificate quashed for deaf Sri Lankan child facing Dublin removal to Germany; educational discontinuity risk arguable.

enrichment.short_title: Jegatheeswaran: SLI child and manifestly unfounded Dublin removal cert
key_facts: K, a 13-year-old Sri Lankan Tamil with deafness and specific language impairment, faced removal to Germany under the Dublin procedure.
He had developed communicative competence in English through intensive UK specialist education after earlier asylum claims in Italy and the UK.
Educational psychologist Ruth Wheeler warned that restarting education in German carried a significant risk he would not communicate functionally in any spoken language.
The Secretary of State maintained a section 72 clearly unfounded certificate denying an in-country appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review of a decision upholding a clearly unfounded certificate in respect of Article 8 grounds against Dublin removal to Germany.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the April 2005 decision that the human rights claim was manifestly unfounded was invalid, entitling K to an in-country appeal to an adjudicator.
enrichment.ratio: Where expert evidence establishes a significant risk that Dublin removal would disrupt specialist language education and leave a deaf child unable to communicate functionally in any spoken language, Article 8 is arguably engaged and the consequences are sufficiently grave that the claim cannot be certified as manifestly unfounded, even in a foreign-case removal context.
legal_issues: Whether removal to Germany would arguably breach K's Article 8 rights
Whether educational discontinuity and language loss risk meets the Razgar threshold
Lawfulness of maintaining a clearly unfounded certificate as evidence evolved
Whether specialist provision in Germany negates the discontinuity argument
linked_authorities: R (Razgar) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] 2 AC 368
R (Bardiqi) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWHC 1788 (Admin)
Bensaid v United Kingdom (2001) 33 EHRR 205

notes: Student fees legitimate expectation JR succeeded on procedural unfairness over mitigation without prior consultation.

enrichment.short_title: Salman v Barking: mistaken student funding advice and legitimate expectation
key_facts: Tanyel Salman enrolled at the private British School of Osteopathy after Barking and Dagenham officers said designated-course fees would be paid subject to a £1,125 contribution.
Three weeks into the course the authority admitted error: private designated courses were not funded on the same basis as public universities.
She rejected other UCAS offers and continued studying pending the authority's response; the school later became publicly funded for later years.
The council offered first-year fees plus £1,000 compensation but relied on failure to mitigate without having raised that before.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a local authority decision refusing full fee funding after erroneous advice, by then largely overtaken by the school's change of status.
enrichment.outcome: Decision of 12 February 2004 unlawful for procedural unfairness in relying on mitigation without prior consultation; authority to reconsider, though the £6,500 offer later covered actual financial loss.
enrichment.ratio: Where a local authority creates a legitimate expectation of funding through mistaken advice on which a student relied in rejecting alternatives, it may make a section 2 payment to remedy the error, but it cannot penalise the student for failing to mitigate unless that point is fairly put before decision so she can respond.
legal_issues: Whether a legitimate expectation of fee funding arose from the authority's advice
Whether the authority had power to pay under section 2 Local Government Act 2000
Whether the student had a duty to mitigate after the error was disclosed
Procedural fairness in relying on mitigation without prior notice
linked_authorities: R (Theophilus) v London Borough of Lewisham

notes: CRHP reference on Southall GMC sanction; three-year child protection condition upheld but wording and Rule 31(5) review held unduly lenient.

enrichment.short_title: CRHP v GMC: Southall child protection condition reference

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service Reform and Health Care Professions Act 2002

key_facts: Professor David Southall, a renowned paediatrician, watched a Channel 4 programme on Sally Clark and reported to police that her husband Stephen Clark had suffocated a child and killed both sons.
He breached Trust restrictions on child protection work and produced a report to the guardian's solicitors presenting theory as near certainty without access to case papers or adequate caveats.
The GMC PCC found serious professional misconduct and imposed a three-year condition excluding all child protection work; the Council for the Regulation of Healthcare Professionals sought erasure.
Extensive testimonials and Dr Chipping's evidence showed a robust NHS system had prevented further child protection involvement since 2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court reference under section 29 of the 2002 Act treated as an appeal against an unduly lenient GMC disciplinary sanction.
enrichment.outcome: Erasure not required; conditional registration was not unduly lenient overall, but the appeal was allowed to require tighter conditions and a Rule 31(5) intimation for review at the end of three years.
enrichment.ratio: On a section 29 reference the test is whether the penalty is one a disciplinary tribunal could reasonably impose having regard to public safety and profession reputation; testimonials and proven monitoring systems may justify conditional registration rather than erasure for serious misconduct, but conditions must be precisely drawn and review mechanisms used where insight remains limited.
legal_issues: Whether erasure was the only appropriate sanction for Southall's misconduct
Application of Ruscillo unduly lenient and manifest inappropriateness tests
Weight to be given to testimonials in GMC sanction decisions
Whether three-year child protection exclusion with review was adequate
linked_authorities: Council for the Regulation of Healthcare Professionals v General Medical Council [2004] EWCA Civ 1356
Bolton v Law Society [1994] 1 WLR 512
Bijl v General Medical Council [2002] Lloyd's Med Rep 60

notes: Clearly unfounded Article 8 certificate upheld for Afghan brother facing Dublin removal despite mentally ill sibling carer.

enrichment.short_title: Ahmadi v SSHD: sibling carer and Dublin removal certificate
key_facts: Fawad Ahmadi, an Afghan illegal entrant, claimed asylum in the UK in August 2004 after prior claims in Germany and Norway; Germany accepted Dublin responsibility.
His brother Zia, a refugee with severe treatment-resistant schizophrenia, had been unable to benefit from a carer until Fawad was released on bail in March 2005.
Psychiatrist Dr Heavey said Fawad's care improved Zia's engagement but separation risked relapse requiring Mental Health Act admission.
The Secretary of State certified Fawad's Article 8 claim as clearly unfounded, blocking an in-country appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review of maintained clearly unfounded certification of Article 8 claims against Dublin removal to Germany, including Zia as second claimant.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; family life since bail was brief and precarious, Zia's case was not truly exceptional under Huang, and Mental Health Act services meant Article 3 was not engaged.
enrichment.ratio: Where siblings were separated for years and family life in the UK existed only briefly after bail in a precarious Dublin removal case, care of a mentally ill relative does not make an Article 8 claim truly exceptional; state mental health compulsory admission powers prevent Article 3 breach if care breaks down.
legal_issues: Whether sibling family life makes Dublin removal disproportionate under Article 8
Application of Huang truly exceptional test outside Immigration Rules
Whether removal would breach the ill brother's Article 3 or Article 8 rights
Effect of brief carer role since bail on certification
linked_authorities: Huang v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2005] EWCA Civ 105
